## 2.1 Variables and assignments (general)

In programming, = is an assignment of a left-side variable with a right-side value.

= IS NOT EQUALS

## 2.2 Variables (int)

Allocation is the process of determining a suitable memory location to store data like variables. Happens during variable declaration.

Expression is just another word for value or operation. Like right side expression.

## 2.3 Identifiers

The name of variables or methods is called an identifier. An identifier must:

- Be a sequence of letters, underscore (), dollar sign($), and digits
- Start with a letter, underscore, or dollar sign
- No spaces. No ! Or ? Or anything.

They are case sensitive.

There are some reserved words. They are a word part of a language, like int or double, that cannot be used as an identifier. Also known as keyword.

While these are valid, there are two main types of coding conventions just for style points:

- Camel case: Lower camel case abuts multiple words, capitalizing each word except the first, as in numApples or peopleOnBus
- Underscore separated: Words are lowercase and separated by an underscore, as in num_apples or people_on_bus

Neither is better/worse. We're using lower camel case just because.

## 2.4 Arithmetic expressions (general)

An expression is any individual item or combination of items.

A literal is a specific value in code like 2.

An operator is a symbol that performs a built-in calculation. Common ones are listed below:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Math is slightly different in code. Unless otherwise specified, it is the same. Differences:

You have to use * to multiply, two variables with no space does not count and neither does something like 2x.

You can use two negative signs in a row or a + then -. The first one represents subtraction/addition, while the second represents a negative number.

An expression is evaluated in the standard order of mathematics, this is called precedence rules.

![](data:image/png;base64,)
#OrderOfEvaluation

Compound operators provide a shorthand way to update a variable. +=, -=, /=, %=

## 2.7 Floating-point numbers (double)

A floating-point number is a real number containing a decimal point that can appear anywhere in the number.

Typically used for measurements (degrees, meters, temp degrees) and fractions of countable items.

Except money, use ints to count cents or dollars because of the money rounding problems

A double stores a floating-point number

A floating-point literal is a number with a fractional part, even if the fraction is 0, as in 1.0, 0.0, or 99.573. Good practice is to always have a digit before the decimal point, even if it's just 0.5.

If you divide a float by 0 it will usually produce an error. In Java it produces infinity or negative infinity.

If they're both 0 the division results in a "not a number". Not a number (NaN) indicates an unrepresented or undefined value.

Most languages will output 5 decimal points. Sometimes this is not necessary. Note, this rounds up. You can output floating-point numbers with a specific number of digits by:

`System.out.printf("%.2f", myFloat);

## 2.14 Characters

To get characters from user input, there's a few extra steps. There is no `scnr.nextChar()` and there also isn't any scnr.nextString(). To get a string from input, use scnr.next(). To get a specific character, do scnr.next().charAt(index)  
NOTE: scnr.next() will skip the initial whitespace and get characters until the NEXT WHITESPACE, then it stops. (looking at it visually, the first space between words). If you put several scnr.next() in a row, they'll each pick up one word and then stop at the space between words (not actually words but its easier to explain it).

To actually get all the text entered including whitespace, use scnr.nextLine(). Note: It does not grab newlines, it stops there. Literally just grabs one line. ALSO NOTE: next() does not pick up newline, so if you have an input with a newline at the end, do next() first, then nextLine(), nextLine() will be blank because the newline is still there but all the text got picked up by next(). You can use an extra nextLine() to skip the newline.

[https://www.asciitable.com](https://www.asciitable.com)

An escape sequence is a two-character sequence starting with \ that represents a special character. For example, \n represents a newline character

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Note: The compiler treats these as the 2nd thing not the \. So the ASCII value for \" is 34 because 34 = 34 "

2.18 Random numbers

If a programmer wants something in a range that starts not at 0, add a number to the randomly generated one.

Like if you want a random int in the range of 10 to 15, do randGen.nextInt(6) + 10 (remember that it generates from 0-n-1, so its 5)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Randomly generated numbers are pseudo-random. The nextInt() method has an equation to compute the next "random" integer from the previous one, (invisibly) keeping track of the previous one. This is seeded using the current time

A programmer can specify the seed when a random object is created by using Random randGen = new Random(5); or using the setSeed() method, as in randGen.setSeed(5); A specific seed will mean that each program run will yield the same sequence of pseudo-random numbers
